question.text: Which of the following is equivalent to $6x \equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\,35)?$
question.explanation:
The scalar multiplication properties of congruences state that for $k \in \mathbb{Z},$ we have the following:

  • $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$

  • $a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\,n) \quad \Longrightarrow\quad ka \equiv kb \:(\textrm{mod}\,kn)$

The modulus equals $35$ in all statements, which suggests we'll need to use the first property.

Notice that the coefficient of $x$ is $6,$ and $6\cdot 6 = 36$ is one larger than the modulus. Therefore, we can reduce the coefficient of $x$ to unity as follows:

\begin{align*} 6x & \equiv 1 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,35) \\[5pt] 6 \cdot 6x & \equiv 6 \cdot 1 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,35) \\[5pt] 36x & \equiv 6 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,35) \\[5pt] x+35x & \equiv 6 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,35) \\[5pt] x+0x & \equiv 6 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,35) \\[5pt] x & \equiv 6 \quad& (\textrm{mod}\,35) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text: By the multiplicative property of congruences, $77 \cdot 82 \equiv $
question.explanation:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

\[ a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n), \]

then, we have

\[ ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

First, we note the following: \begin{align*} 77 &\equiv 12\cdot 6 + 5 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv12\cdot 0 + 5 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] & \equiv {\color{red}{5}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[10pt] 82 &\equiv 13\cdot 6 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv13\cdot 0 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] & \equiv {\color{blue}{4}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \end{align*}

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 77 \cdot 82 &\equiv {\color{red}{5}} \cdot {\color{blue}{4}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 20\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 3\cdot 6 + 2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 3\cdot 0+2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ 77 \cdot 82 \equiv 2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,6). \]

question.text: Use the multiplicative property of congruences to compute the following residue.
question.explanation:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

\[ a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n), \]

then, we have

\[ ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

\[ 8^{6} = 8^2\cdot 8^2\cdot 8^2. \]

Next, we note the following:

\begin{align*} 8^2 &\equiv 64 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5) \\[5pt] &\equiv 12\cdot 5 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5)\\[5pt] &\equiv 12\cdot 0 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{4}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5)\\[10pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 8^{6} &\equiv 8^2 \cdot 8^2\cdot 8^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{4}}\cdot {\color{blue}{4}} \cdot {\color{blue}{4}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5) \\[5pt] &\equiv 64 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\,5) \\[5pt] &\equiv 12\cdot 5 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5)\\[5pt] &\equiv 12\cdot 0 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5)\\[5pt] &\equiv 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 5) \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ 8^{6} \textrm{ mod } 5 = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{4}. \]

question.text: By the multiplicative property of congruences, $4^{8}\equiv$
question.explanation:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

\[ a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n), \]

then, we have

\[ ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

\[ 4^{8} = 4^3 \cdot 4^3\cdot 4^2. \]

Next, we note the following:

\begin{align*} 4^2 &\equiv 16 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 2\cdot 7 + 2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 2\cdot 0 + 2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{2}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[10pt] 4^3 &\equiv 4\cdot 4^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 4\cdot {\color{blue}2} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv 8 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] & \equiv 1 \cdot 7 +1\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] & \equiv 1 \cdot 0 +1\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{red}{1}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7) \end{align*}

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 4^{8} &\equiv 4^2\cdot 4^3 \cdot 4^3 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{2}}\cdot {\color{red}{1}}\cdot {\color{red}{1}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7) \\[5pt] &\equiv 2\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 7) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ 4^{8} \equiv 2 \qquad\qquad (\textrm{mod}\,7). \]

The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if \[ a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n), \]

then, we have \[ ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example, \[ 12^{4} = (3 \cdot 4)^4 = 3^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 4^2\cdot 4^2. \]

Next, we note the following: \begin{align*} 3^2 &\equiv 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8) \\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 8 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8)\\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 0 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{1}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8)\\[10pt] 4^2 &\equiv 16 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8) \\[5pt] &\equiv 2\cdot 8 + 0 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8)\\[5pt] &\equiv 2\cdot 0 + 0 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{red}{0}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 0) \end{align*}

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following: \begin{align*} 12^{4} &\equiv 3^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 4^2\cdot 4^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{1}} \cdot {\color{blue}{1}} \cdot {\color{red}{0}}\cdot {\color{red}{0}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 8) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.explanation:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

\[ a\equiv b \quad \textrm{and}\quad c\equiv d \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n), \]

then, we have

\[ ac\equiv bd \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n). \]

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

\[ 21^{4} = (3\cdot 7)^4 = 3^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 7^2\cdot 7^2. \]

Next, we note the following:

\begin{align*} 3^2 &\equiv 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 6 + 3 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 0 + 3 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{red}{3}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[10pt] 7^2 &\equiv 49 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv 8\cdot 6 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv 8\cdot 0 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{1}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \end{align*}

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 21^{4} &\equiv 3^2\cdot 3^2\cdot 7^2\cdot 7^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{red}{3}} \cdot {\color{red}{3}}\cdot {\color{blue}{1}}\cdot {\color{blue}{1}}\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 9\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 6 + 3\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 0 + 3\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] &\equiv 3\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 6) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text: What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of $14^{14}?$
question.explanation:
If $a\equiv b\:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c\equiv d\:(\textrm{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

  • $ac\equiv bd \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$

  • $a^k \equiv b^k \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue: \[ 14^{14} \textrm{ mod } 10 \]

First, we note the following:

\begin{align*} 14 &\equiv 10+4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 0 + 4 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{red}4} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \end{align*}

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 14^2 &\equiv {\color{red}4}^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] &\equiv 16 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] & \equiv 10 + 6\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] & \equiv 0 + 6\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{6}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[10pt] 14^6&\equiv \left(14^2\right)^3 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{6}}^3 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 216 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] & \equiv 21\cdot 10 + 6 &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] & \equiv 21\cdot 0 + 6 &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{purple}{6}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \end{align*}

Next, we decompose $14^{14}$ into a product of smaller exponents.

\[ 14^{14} = \left(14^6\right)^2\cdot 14^2 \]

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 14^{14} &\equiv \left(14^6\right)^2 \cdot 14^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv ({\color{purple}{6}})^2\cdot {\color{blue}{6}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 216 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 21 \cdot 10 + 6\qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] & \equiv 21\cdot 0 + 6 &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 6 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ 14^{14} \textrm{ mod } 10 = 6 \]

which means that the last digit of $14^{14}$ is $6.$

question.text: What is the last digit in the decimal expansion of $29^{13}?$
question.explanation:
If $a\equiv b\:(\textrm{mod}\,n)$ and $c\equiv d\:(\textrm{mod}\,n),$ then the following properties hold:

  • $ac\equiv bd \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$

  • $a^k \equiv b^k \: (\textrm{mod}\,n)$ for any positive integer $k$

To find the last digit, we need to calculate the following residue: \[ 29^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10 \]

First, we note the following:

\begin{align*} 29 &\equiv 20+9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 2\cdot 10 + 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 2\cdot 0 + 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{red}{9}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \end{align*}

Therefore, by the exponentiation property, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 29^2 &\equiv {\color{red}{9}}^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] &\equiv 81 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 8\cdot 10 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 8\cdot 0 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv \color{blue}{1} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \end{align*}

Next, we decompose $29^{13}$ into a product of smaller exponents.

\[ 29^{13} = \left(29^2\right)^6\cdot 29 \]

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 29^{13} &\equiv \left(29^2\right)^6\cdot 29 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv ({\color{blue}{1}})^6\cdot {\color{red}{9}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ 29^{13} \textrm{ mod } 10 =9 \]

which means that the last digit of $29^{13}$ is $9.$

\begin{align*} 17^2 &\equiv {\color{red}{7}}^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] &\equiv 49 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 4\cdot 10 + 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 4\cdot 0 + 9 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{blue}{9}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[10pt] 17^4 & \equiv ({\color{blue}{9}})^2 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10)\\[5pt] &\equiv 81 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 8\cdot 10 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 8\cdot 0 + 1 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv {\color{purple}{1}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \end{align*}

Next, we decompose $17^{21}$ into a product of smaller exponents.

\[ 17^{21} = \left(17^4\right)^5 \cdot 17 \]

By applying the multiplicative and exponentiation properties, we have the following:

\begin{align*} 17^{21} &\equiv \left(17^4\right)^5\cdot 17 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv ({\color{red}{1}})^5\cdot {\color{purple}{7}} \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 1\cdot 7 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] &\equiv 7 \qquad &(\textrm{mod}\, 10) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we conclude that

\[ 17^{21} \textrm{ mod } 10 = 7 \]

which means that the last digit of $17^{21}$ is $7.$
